whoa.headline: A day on Venus is longer than its year
whoa.summary: Venus spins so slowly that one turn takes longer than one trip around the Sun. Sunrise there is a rare event.
whoa.try: Earth: 24 hours. Venus: about 243 Earth days. Say that out loud.
whoa.tryLine: Earth: 24 hours. Venus: about 243 Earth days. Say that out loud.

whoa.headline: A straw works because of air, not magic suck
whoa.summary: You lower the pressure in your mouth. Outside air pushes the drink up the straw. Space has no air push, so straws fail there.
whoa.try: Pinch the top of a full straw. The drink stays. That's air pressure.
whoa.tryLine: Pinch the top of a full straw. The drink stays. That's air pressure.

whoa.headline: She spotted a supernova at 14
whoa.summary: Caroline Moore was 14 when she found an exploding star in another galaxy. She used a backyard-style telescope network and careful checking. Pro astronomers confirmed it.
whoa.try: Look up 'supernova' images. That's a star's last big shout.
whoa.tryLine: Look up 'supernova' images. That's a star's last big shout.

whoa.headline: Fold a T-shirt in two seconds
whoa.summary: Pinch the shoulder and the mid-chest, flip it over the other shoulder, then fold. Once you have the pinch points, it looks like a trick.
whoa.try: Race a messy pile. Time the first three shirts.
whoa.tryLine: Race a messy pile. Time the first three shirts.

whoa.headline: You interrupted and the room went quiet
whoa.summary: Own it fast: 'Sorry - finish your bit.' Then wait. That one line turns an oops into respect.
whoa.try: Practise it once so it is ready when you need it.
whoa.tryLine: Practise it once so it is ready when you need it.

whoa.headline: Penguins propose with a pebble
whoa.summary: Some penguins hunt for a smooth pebble and drop it at a partner's feet. If the pebble is accepted, that is a yes. Romance, but rocky.
whoa.try: If you see penguins in a film, watch for the pebble handover.
whoa.tryLine: If you see penguins in a film, watch for the pebble handover.

whoa.headline: Your body makes a new skeleton every 10 years
whoa.summary: Bone is not a dead stick. Cells nibble old bone and lay new bone. The skeleton you have at 20 is not the same material you had at 10.
whoa.try: Jump. That's the system answering back.
whoa.tryLine: Jump. That's the system answering back.

whoa.headline: Learn one useful knot: the bowline
whoa.summary: The bowline makes a loop that does not slip. Boats, trees, and rescue lines use it. Rabbit out the hole, around the tree, back down.
whoa.try: YouTube 'bowline' with a shoelace. Make three in a row.
whoa.tryLine: YouTube 'bowline' with a shoelace. Make three in a row.

whoa.headline: He built a Braille printer from Lego
whoa.summary: Shubham Banerjee was 13 when he made a cheap Braille printer using Lego Mindstorms so more kids could afford books they can feel.
whoa.try: Close your eyes and read a cereal box by shape. Hard, right?
whoa.tryLine: Close your eyes and read a cereal box by shape. Hard, right?

whoa.headline: Velcro is a burr that said yes
whoa.summary: A Swiss engineer pulled burrs off his dog and looked under a microscope. Tiny hooks. He copied them. Your trainers are wearing a plant idea.
whoa.try: Find a burr on a walk. That's the original Velcro.
whoa.tryLine: Find a burr on a walk. That's the original Velcro.

whoa.headline: Someone is left out at lunch
whoa.summary: You do not need a speech. 'Want to sit with us?' is enough. If they say no, you still planted a door.
whoa.try: Use it once this week. One sentence.
whoa.tryLine: Use it once this week. One sentence.

whoa.headline: A teaspoon of a neutron star would weigh a mountain
whoa.summary: The leftover core of a giant star is packed past imagining. A spoon of it would weigh billions of tonnes. Gravity won that argument.
whoa.try: Hold a teaspoon. Now imagine it weighing more than everyone you know.
whoa.tryLine: Hold a teaspoon. Now imagine it weighing more than everyone you know.

whoa.headline: An octopus has three hearts
whoa.summary: Two hearts pump blood to the gills. The third pumps blood to the rest of the body - and it actually stops when the octopus swims.
whoa.try: Ask someone: why would a heart stop on purpose?
whoa.tryLine: Ask someone: why would a heart stop on purpose?

whoa.headline: Planes don't float. They steal lift from air.
whoa.summary: The wing is curved so air on top moves faster and pushes less. Air underneath pushes more, and that extra push is lift. Same idea as holding your hand out a car window.
whoa.try: Next car ride, tilt your hand like a wing and feel it climb.
whoa.tryLine: Next car ride, tilt your hand like a wing and feel it climb.

whoa.headline: A 14-year-old built a windmill from scrap
whoa.summary: William Kamkwamba's village in Malawi had almost no electricity. He used a library book, a broken bicycle, and junkyard parts. The windmill lit his house and pumped water.
whoa.try: What broken thing in your house could still do a job?
whoa.tryLine: What broken thing in your house could still do a job?

whoa.headline: Tell if an egg is still good in 5 seconds
whoa.summary: Drop it in a glass of water. Fresh eggs sink and lie on their side. Old eggs stand up. Bad eggs float - throw those away.
whoa.try: Test one egg from the fridge tonight.
whoa.tryLine: Test one egg from the fridge tonight.

whoa.headline: Your friend got the part you wanted
whoa.summary: First feeling: unfair. Good move: "Congrats. You earned it." Then ask the teacher what to practise for next time. You look strong, and you get a plan.
whoa.try: Practise that one line out loud. It feels weird. That's normal.
whoa.tryLine: Practise that one line out loud. It feels weird. That's normal.

whoa.headline: You cannot tickle yourself. Your brain blocks you.
whoa.summary: Your brain predicts your own fingers, so the surprise is gone. Tickling needs a tiny "I didn't see that coming." That's why another person works and you don't.
whoa.try: Try it anyway. Then try to tickle a parent who isn't ready.
whoa.tryLine: Try it anyway. Then try to tickle a parent who isn't ready.

whoa.headline: A lightning bolt is hotter than the surface of the sun
whoa.summary: The sun's surface is about 5,500°C. A lightning bolt can hit 30,000°C. That's why it turns air into a flash and a boom you hear later.
whoa.try: Next storm, count the seconds after the flash. Divide by 3 for kilometres.
whoa.tryLine: Next storm, count the seconds after the flash. Divide by 3 for kilometres.

whoa.headline: She built a flashlight that runs on body heat
whoa.summary: Ann Makosinski was 15. She made a hollow flashlight with no batteries - just the heat from your hand. It won a big science fair and actually worked.
whoa.try: Hold a metal spoon. Notice it feels colder than wood. That's heat leaving your hand.
whoa.tryLine: Hold a metal spoon. Notice it feels colder than wood. That's heat leaving your hand.

whoa.headline: A lock is just a bunch of tiny lifts
whoa.summary: Your key is a row of hills. Each hill lifts a pin to the exact right height so the cylinder can turn. Wrong key = one pin still blocking.
whoa.try: Look at a house key. Those jagged bits are the hills.
whoa.tryLine: Look at a house key. Those jagged bits are the hills.

whoa.headline: The 60-second room reset
whoa.summary: Set a timer. Clothes on the chair, rubbish in the bin, stuff you used back where it lives. Don't clean. Just reset. Most rooms look 80% better in one minute.
whoa.try: Do it once tonight. See if it feels like a magic trick.
whoa.tryLine: Do it once tonight. See if it feels like a magic trick.

whoa.headline: Someone laughs at your idea
whoa.summary: Don't laugh at yourself to join in. Try: "Okay, but I'm still going to try it." Short. Calm. You didn't attack them, and you didn't drop the idea.
whoa.try: Use it on something small this week, even a game idea.
whoa.tryLine: Use it on something small this week, even a game idea.

whoa.headline: Your brain dumps the mission mid-walk
whoa.summary: You stand up, walk into a room, and forget why. Doorways actually reset a bit of your memory. Your brain files "kitchen plan" and starts "hallway plan."
whoa.try: Say the mission out loud before you walk. "Glass of water." It sticks better.
whoa.tryLine: Say the mission out loud before you walk. "Glass of water." It sticks better.

whoa.headline: "Look up at the stars and not down at your feet."
whoa.summary: Stephen Hawking said that. He meant: spend your brain on big, interesting things, not on small worries. You can do both in one night - homework, then 2 minutes of sky.
whoa.try: Tonight, step outside and find one thing in the sky you can name.
whoa.tryLine: Tonight, step outside and find one thing in the sky you can name.

whoa.headline: Tardigrades can survive outer space
whoa.summary: These tiny "water bears" can dry out, freeze, and even go into space with no suit - then wake up later and walk around. They are almost impossible to kill.
whoa.try: Look up a tardigrade photo. It looks like a chubby eight-legged bear.
whoa.tryLine: Look up a tardigrade photo. It looks like a chubby eight-legged bear.

whoa.headline: At 13 he built a radio station from junk
whoa.summary: Kelvin Doe lived in Sierra Leone with almost no money for parts. He made batteries from acid, soda and metal, then a transmitter from scrap. Neighbours tuned in to his station for music and local news. MIT later invited him to show how he did it.
whoa.try: Pick one broken gadget at home. Can you name 3 parts inside it?
whoa.tryLine: Pick one broken gadget at home. Can you name 3 parts inside it?

whoa.headline: The game already started without you
whoa.summary: Don't hover. Walk up and say "Got room for one more?" If they say not this round: "Cool, I'll jump in next." Then watch like a teammate, not like a sad statue.
whoa.try: Use it at break. The sentence is the whole trick.
whoa.tryLine: Use it at break. The sentence is the whole trick.

whoa.headline: Wi - Fi is just shouted numbers, very fast
whoa.summary: Your router yells invisible radio blips. Your phone listens and turns the blips back into pictures and words. Walls eat some of the yell, which is why the signal dies in the bathroom.
whoa.try: Stand next to the router, then behind a wall. Watch the bars change.
whoa.tryLine: Stand next to the router, then behind a wall. Watch the bars change.

whoa.headline: Cows pick a best friend - and stay calmer together
whoa.summary: Scientists found many cows choose one favourite cow and hang out with them. Smart farms keep those pairs together, because friend-cows eat better and stay healthier. Even cows know a good teammate helps.
whoa.try: Next time you see cows, watch who stands next to who.
whoa.tryLine: Next time you see cows, watch who stands next to who.

whoa.headline: Remember any name with one trick
whoa.summary: When you meet someone, say their name back once: "Cool, I'm ___, hi Maya." Then stick it to a picture in your head - Maya with a map. People light up when you get it right next time.
whoa.try: Use it on one new person this week. Just the repeat is enough.
whoa.tryLine: Use it on one new person this week. Just the repeat is enough.

whoa.headline: There are more trees on Earth than stars in our galaxy
whoa.summary: The Milky Way has around 100 billion stars. Earth has about 3 trillion trees. We still cut them down too fast - but the planet is greener and stranger than it looks from a car.
whoa.try: Guess how many trees you can see from your window. Then count.
whoa.tryLine: Guess how many trees you can see from your window. Then count.

whoa.headline: Hunt: one free kids thing this week
whoa.summary: Libraries, museums and parks quietly run free drop-ins. Pick one, show up, stay 20 minutes. That counts as an adventure.
whoa.try: Ask a parent to search free kids events this weekend plus your town.
whoa.tryLine: Ask a parent to search free kids events this weekend plus your town.

whoa.headline: Four astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space
whoa.summary: Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.

whoa.headline: Inside the King's private gardens at his Highgrove home
whoa.summary: See what happened when De-Graft was invited to join His Majesty the King's gardening team in his private garden at Highgrove House.

whoa.headline: Quiz of the Week: Have you been following this week's news?
whoa.summary: It's been a busy week of big stories and headlines. Have you been keeping up with the news over the last seven days? Test your knowledge of the latest top stories with our Quiz of the Week.

whoa.headline: Strange News: The weirdest stories of the week
whoa.summary: Shanequa has this week's Strange News, including very elaborate nail art, giant hailstones and a special delivery robot.

whoa.headline: Crew-12 Returns to Earth
whoa.summary: The SpaceX Crew Dragon Freedom spacecraft is seen as it lands with NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev aboard in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Los Angeles, Calif., Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026.

whoa.headline: Astronomers pinpoint the most distant fast radio burst ever detected
whoa.summary: Astronomers have detected and traced the most distant fast radio burst ever recorded, a powerful flash of radio waves that traveled for more than 10 billion years across the cosmos before reaching Earth.

whoa.headline: These clues might point to life on other worlds
whoa.summary: Lead-melting temperatures on the surface of Venus should make life as we know it impossible there. But scientists have detected some curious chemicals in clouds above the planet's surface. At those heights, temps and pressures would be similar to those on Earth.

whoa.headline: Some germs ride a superhighway at the edge of space
whoa.summary: The stratosphere is both beautiful and deadly - a boundary between Earth and space, between life and death. Hover within it, some 30 kilometers (almost 20 miles) above the ground, and you'd be nearly twice as high as any rain cloud. You would actually see the edges of Earth curve beneath you.

whoa.headline: Solar Orbiter tracks origin of mysterious magnetic switchbacks
whoa.summary: The European Space Agency-led Solar Orbiter spacecraft has flown through an S-shaped kink known as a 'switchback' in the solar wind's magnetic field. By fingerprinting the elusive particles within the switchback, Solar Orbiter has traced its origin back to the Sun's surface and revealed more about solar magnetism - the unruly instigator of dangerous solar storms.

whoa.headline: "It's not too late": New report says 'Science of Hope' is key to stopping wildlife loss
whoa.summary: The WWF's Chief Scientific Advisor Mike Barrett told Newsround that nature is "in big trouble" around the world, but "we have still got solutions to put it right".

whoa.headline: Artemis II crew moon photo annotations
whoa.summary: A visualization of a dark moon eclipsing the sun is marked with handwritten notes in this April 6, 2026, screenshot from an Artemis II crew member's tablet.

whoa.headline: Undergraduate student may have solved puzzle regarding isolated galaxies that have stopped producing stars
whoa.summary: An undergraduate astrophysics student at UC Berkeley has found three unusual galaxies - cataloged as Shapiro Dwarf Galaxies I, II and III. Each galaxy is far from other galaxies and has stopped making stars, a combination that is extremely rare. The discovery, published in The Astrophysical Journal, provides compelling observational evidence of a long-held astronomical theory.

whoa.headline: Five Discoveries That Changed Our Understanding of T. Rex Forever, From Warm Blood to Lips
whoa.summary: Paleontologists are still unraveling the secrets of the world's most famous dinosaur, such as its outward appearance or the way that it hunted. With each new finding, our view of the "tyrant lizard king" has gotten a little clearer - and sometimes has radically shifted

whoa.headline: "There's so much biodiversity" Otis finds out what lives in Liverpool docks
whoa.summary: Dockwatch is a project run by World Museum Liverpool and the Canal and River Trust that gives people a chance to see what lives in the water or Albert dock in Liverpool. Otis went to find out more.

whoa.headline: Artemis II Crew Moon Photo Annotations
whoa.summary: A visualization of a dark Moon eclipsing the Sun is marked with handwritten notes in this April 6, 2026, screenshot from an Artemis II crew member's tablet.

whoa.headline: Mars's oddest cloud may be even odder than we thought
whoa.summary: Scientists using the European Space Agency's Mars Express , in combination with a state-of-the-art meteorological model of the Red Planet, have found that there may be some very exotic physics behind Mars's most curious cloud.

whoa.headline: Meet the first teacher in Scotland to give lessons just about AI
whoa.summary: The special role is brand new at a secondary school in East Renfrewshire, and pupils have been volunteering to help him find the best way to teach the subject.

whoa.headline: Experiment: Discover the science behind afterimages
whoa.summary: Objective: Investigate color perception by observing afterimages, which are the images left on your retina after you stare at an object and then look away. Areas of Science: Human Biology & Health Difficulty: Intermediate medium Time required: Short (2-5 days) Prerequisites: A computer with internet access is recommended. Material availability: Readily available Cost: Very Low (under $20) Safety: No issues Credits: David Whyte, PhD, Science Buddies We perceive color in the world around us with special sensory cells, called cone cells .

whoa.headline: Physicists may have finally glimpsed elusive dark matter
whoa.summary: One day in June 2023, the many unblinking, electronic eyes of the LUX-ZEPLIN detector - LZ for short - may have glimpsed something remarkable. They may have made the first direct detection of dark matter . @sciencenewsofficial Scientists think dark matter is everywhere in space, but no one has ever actually seen it.

whoa.headline: Computer scientist tracks satellites with automated observatory built from off-the-shelf technology
whoa.summary: Allen Schnibben's interest in space started when he was a child. "I picked up some books about the solar system when I was in elementary school. In middle school, I got a telescope and I started observing the night sky as a hobby," said Schnibben, a computer scientist at Sandia National Laboratories.

whoa.headline: Simulated moon soil and recyclable thermoplastics could help build future space infrastructure
whoa.summary: Transporting material from Earth to the moon is an expensive proposition: By some estimates, moving a single kilogram (2.2 pounds) can cost more than $1 million. Any plan to build a permanent human habitat up there will depend on bringing that sky-high cost down.

whoa.headline: Your Planet: Environmental news from around the world
whoa.summary: This week on Your Planet, we find out why pelicans need help in Peru, spot leopards in South Africa and meet thousands of baby turtles being released in Turkey.

whoa.headline: Astronomers Solve Cosmic Cold Case with NASA Hubble Data
whoa.summary: This artist's concept depicts a possible explanation for the unusual chemical abundances NASA's Hubble Space Telescope detected in the HS 0209+0832 system: a second-generation planet orbiting the white dwarf star.

whoa.headline: Webb captures commotion from nebula's stellar jets
whoa.summary: Image: Webb captures commotion from nebula's stellar jets

whoa.headline: Let's learn about origami-inspired science
whoa.summary: People have used origami for centuries to transform flat pieces of paper into 2-D and 3-D shapes. In minutes, a beginner can use this Japanese art of paper folding to craft simple birds, flowers and jumping frogs . More advanced patterns can give rise to highly detailed sculptures of all manner of objects.

whoa.headline: Why are students in France protesting?
whoa.summary: Students have been blocking school entrances and some of the protests have lead to unrest and clashes between police and demonstrators.

whoa.headline: UK gets its very first Comic Town but what does it mean?
whoa.summary: Barrow in Furness in Cumbria has become the UK's very first Comic Town. So what is that and what does it mean for the children living there?

whoa.headline: Neutrons, rotating black holes, and a galactic PeVatron at the center of the Milky Way
whoa.summary: Galactic black holes are cosmic mitochondria, powerhouses of the universe. Most of the energy these supermassive black holes produce comes from the material surrounding them: superheated plasma in their accretion disks interacting with tremendous magnetic fields. But there is a more direct way to extract energy from a black hole.

whoa.headline: Quantum interactions may have locked early universe's fields into existing energy states
whoa.summary: The universe may be trapped in its own comfort zone, and a researcher in the College of Engineering and Computer Science has helped explain why it cannot seem to leave. A new study suggests the universe could be locked into its current state by the same kinds of quantum effects that scientists study when trying to preserve fragile information inside a quantum computer.

whoa.headline: NASA Astronaut Christina Koch at Eagles vs. Rams
whoa.summary: NASA astronaut and mission specialist of the agency's Artemis II mission, Christina Koch, led the fans in singing the Eagles Fight Song from the field at an NFL game between the Philadelphia Eagles and the Los Angeles Rams at Lincoln Financial Field on Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026, in Philadelphia.

whoa.headline: 2026's El Niño is record-breaking - and it's not done yet
whoa.summary: Since June, scientists have been warning that Earth might experience an El Niño unlike any other . It now appears they were right. The periodic climate beast that emerged this year is stronger than any ever seen.

whoa.headline: Scientists Say: Pyrolysis
whoa.summary: Pyrolysis (noun, "Py-RAW-leh-sis") Pyrolysis is a process though which heat breaks down large molecules into smaller ones. It is just one of the chemical reactions that occurs when something is burning. Picture a campfire.

whoa.headline: Who was the first celebrity to leave Strictly?
whoa.summary: Actress Jaime Winstone and celebrity hair stylist Chris Appleton ended up in the bottom two - but who survived to see another week?

whoa.headline: Happy News: Stories to make you smile
whoa.summary: De-Graft has this week's Happy News. We are visiting an autumnal festival in Vietnam, a community garden in Australia and meeting some showbiz pumpkins in Germany.

whoa.headline: Gamma-ray search sets new limits on dark matter annihilation in the inner Milky Way
whoa.summary: Dark matter could be a type of matter in the universe that does not emit, absorb or reflect detectable light and appears to interact very weakly with regular matter. Although physicists have observed gravitational effects attributed to dark matter, they have not yet been able to determine what it is made of.

whoa.headline: Hidden X-ray phase revealed in likely neutron star merger
whoa.summary: An international team of astronomers, including researchers from the Department of Physics and the Hong Kong Institute for Astronomy and Astrophysics (HKIAA) at The University of Hong Kong (HKU), has discovered a previously hidden phase of high-energy activity following the merger of compact stars.

whoa.headline: NASA's DAVINCI Probe Can Stand the Heat
whoa.summary: An engineering model of NASA's DAVINCI (Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble gases, Chemistry, and Imaging) descent probe passed a key test that ran from Aug. 28 to Sept. 10, showing it can survive the extreme temperatures of Venus.

whoa.headline: Ancient Pottery Reveals the Earliest Known Traces of Chocolate East of the Mississippi, Painting a Picture of Connection in the Americas
whoa.summary: A new archaeological discovery suggests that people in present-day Georgia have feasted with cacao for 1,000 years

whoa.headline: These 15 Adorable Photos of Pandas Will Make You Want to Visit the Zoo Immediately
whoa.summary: Members of the fluffy and adorable but vulnerable species are often cared for in zoos and breeding centers around the world, and these snapshots may make you jealous of the caretakers' jobs

whoa.headline: Among naked mole-rats, a royal's scent keeps the peace
whoa.summary: Imagine a superhero that can release a smell so pungent that its enemies stop fighting. For naked mole-rats, the queen wields such power. Naked mole-rat queens release a calming scent to control their colonies , a new study shows.

whoa.headline: Slimy suspects blamed for broken traffic lights
whoa.summary: Traffic lights in Stretford in Greater Manchester kept stopping working, even after engineers fixed or replaced them. Follow the mystery here.

whoa.headline: Strictly movie week: Exclusive pics of the Zootropolis pro dance
whoa.summary: All 15 couples will take part in this year's movie week - and we've got exclusive pics of what's to come!

whoa.headline: Astronauts arrive at International Space Station on the quickest US express flight yet
whoa.summary: Four astronauts pulled up at the International Space Station on Thursday after launching on an eight-hour express that set a U.S. speed record.

whoa.headline: Webb provides crash course on planet-shattering collisions
whoa.summary: In the early history of our solar system, scientists theorize that a Mars-sized object called Theia smashed into the infant Earth, vaporizing massive amounts of rock and blasting it into space. Some of that material coalesced into the moon, where NASA's Artemis program is returning humans, preparing for Mars and shaping the future of space exploration.

whoa.headline: NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 Launches
whoa.summary: A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying the company's Dragon spacecraft is launched on NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station with NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov aboard, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.

whoa.headline: Farting fish and tooting manatees - how some animals use gas
whoa.summary: Humans aren't the only animals who fart. Take Dakota, an English cocker spaniel. When she was getting older, she could no longer hold in her gas, says Em Finke, Dakota's former human.

whoa.headline: Burps and farts: Why the body is such a gas
whoa.summary: One recent morning, as I was getting ready for the day, I carefully snapped a small sensor to my underwear - right under my butt. Then I worked out, did a full day at my job and hung out with friends. Meanwhile, the tiny sensor in my pants was tracking every single time I farted.

wins.headline: The ozone hole is shrinking
wins.summary: Countries banned the chemicals that were eating the sky's sunscreen. Scientists now measure the hole getting smaller. A giant problem, slowly reversing.
wins.try: The move was a treaty plus better fridges. Teamwork at planet scale.
wins.tryLine: The move was a treaty plus better fridges. Teamwork at planet scale.

wins.headline: Humpback whales came back from the brink
wins.summary: Hunting nearly wiped them out. Bans and watchers gave them decades of quiet. Many populations have rebounded enough that boats now have to share the water.
wins.try: If you ever whale-watch, look for the tail fluke. Each one is unique.
wins.tryLine: If you ever whale-watch, look for the tail fluke. Each one is unique.

wins.headline: Kids' blood lead levels crashed
wins.summary: Lead in petrol and paint used to quietly hurt brains. Laws pulled it out. Average levels in many countries fell hard. Policy can be a superpower.
wins.try: Old houses can still have lead paint. That's a grown-up check, not a kid job.
wins.tryLine: Old houses can still have lead paint. That's a grown-up check, not a kid job.

wins.headline: Humans wiped one killer disease off Earth
wins.summary: Smallpox used to scar and kill millions. Vaccines plus a worldwide hunt ended it in 1980. It is the only human disease we have fully erased.
wins.try: That is what 'the plan worked' looks like at planet size.
wins.tryLine: That is what 'the plan worked' looks like at planet size.

wins.headline: Some rivers got otters back
wins.summary: Cleaner water and protection let otters return to rivers that were empty. If you see one, that's a report card for the whole valley.
wins.try: A local wildlife page will tell you if otters live near you.
wins.tryLine: A local wildlife page will tell you if otters live near you.

wins.headline: Solar got cheap enough to flood the grid
wins.summary: Panels used to be a rich-country toy. Prices crashed. Now whole countries add solar faster than coal. The physics did not change. The cost did.
wins.try: Spot three roofs with panels on your next walk.
wins.tryLine: Spot three roofs with panels on your next walk.

wins.headline: Kids ran a little free library street
wins.summary: A box on a lawn. Take a book, leave a book. Some streets now have three. No app, no fee, just neighbours trusting kids with stories.
wins.try: If you pass one, swap one book. That's the whole game.
wins.tryLine: If you pass one, swap one book. That's the whole game.

wins.headline: Some coral is being grown in nurseries
wins.summary: Divers farm hardy coral and glue it back onto damaged reef. Not a full fix. It is a start, and fish move back in.
wins.try: Reef-safe sunscreen exists. That's a tiny assist.
wins.tryLine: Reef-safe sunscreen exists. That's a tiny assist.

wins.headline: Cities that built bike lanes got more bikes
wins.summary: Paint and kerbs changed who dared to ride. Kids included. Safer paths, more riders, fewer cars on short trips. Design beats nagging.
wins.try: Count bike lanes on your school route. Zero is a clue.
wins.tryLine: Count bike lanes on your school route. Zero is a clue.

wins.headline: Bag charges slashed plastic at the till
wins.summary: A few pence changed habits faster than posters. Many countries saw single-use bags crash. Small price, huge pile of plastic not made.
wins.try: Keep one tote by the door. Future-you will grab it.
wins.tryLine: Keep one tote by the door. Future-you will grab it.

wins.headline: A teen built a cheaper hearing test
wins.summary: Julian Wilson and others have built simple phone-based hearing checks so more kids get spotted early. Not a hospital. A screen and a plan.
wins.try: If someone talks loud at you a lot, a hearing check is kindness, not teasing.
wins.tryLine: If someone talks loud at you a lot, a hearing check is kindness, not teasing.

wins.headline: Beavers got invited back on purpose

wins.summary: Warmer, downward lamps cut glare. Stars came back. Turtles and owls got a quieter night. You can still see the pavement.

wins.summary: Some schools asked pupils to map the boring bits, then rebuild. More climbing, more shade, fewer 'don't'. Behaviour got better because the place got better.

harvest.headline: These clues might point to life on other worlds
harvest.summary: Lead-melting temperatures on the surface of Venus should make life as we know it impossible there. But scientists have detected some curious chemicals in clouds above the planet's surface. At those heights, temps and pressures would be similar to those on Earth.

harvest.headline: Some germs ride a superhighway at the edge of space
harvest.summary: The stratosphere is both beautiful and deadly - a boundary between Earth and space, between life and death. Hover within it, some 30 kilometers (almost 20 miles) above the ground, and you'd be nearly twice as high as any rain cloud. You would actually see the edges of Earth curve beneath you.

harvest.headline: Solar Orbiter tracks origin of mysterious magnetic switchbacks
harvest.summary: The European Space Agency-led Solar Orbiter spacecraft has flown through an S-shaped kink known as a 'switchback' in the solar wind's magnetic field. By fingerprinting the elusive particles within the switchback, Solar Orbiter has traced its origin back to the Sun's surface and revealed more about solar magnetism - the unruly instigator of dangerous solar storms.

harvest.headline: Five Discoveries That Changed Our Understanding of T. Rex Forever, From Warm Blood to Lips
harvest.summary: Paleontologists are still unraveling the secrets of the world's most famous dinosaur, such as its outward appearance or the way that it hunted. With each new finding, our view of the "tyrant lizard king" has gotten a little clearer - and sometimes has radically shifted

harvest.headline: Mars's oddest cloud may be even odder than we thought
harvest.summary: Scientists using the European Space Agency's Mars Express , in combination with a state-of-the-art meteorological model of the Red Planet, have found that there may be some very exotic physics behind Mars's most curious cloud.

harvest.headline: Experiment: Discover the science behind afterimages
harvest.summary: Objective: Investigate color perception by observing afterimages, which are the images left on your retina after you stare at an object and then look away. Areas of Science: Human Biology & Health Difficulty: Intermediate medium Time required: Short (2-5 days) Prerequisites: A computer with internet access is recommended. Material availability: Readily available Cost: Very Low (under $20) Safety: No issues Credits: David Whyte, PhD, Science Buddies We perceive color in the world around us with special sensory cells, called cone cells .

harvest.summary: A new archaeological discovery suggests that people in present-day Georgia have feasted with cacao for 1,000 years

harvest.headline: These 15 Adorable Photos of Pandas Will Make You Want to Visit the Zoo Immediately
harvest.summary: Members of the fluffy and adorable but vulnerable species are often cared for in zoos and breeding centers around the world, and these snapshots may make you jealous of the caretakers' jobs

harvest.headline: Four astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space
harvest.summary: Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.

harvest.headline: Inside the King's private gardens at his Highgrove home
harvest.summary: See what happened when De-Graft was invited to join His Majesty the King's gardening team in his private garden at Highgrove House.

harvest.headline: Quiz of the Week: Have you been following this week's news?
harvest.summary: It's been a busy week of big stories and headlines. Have you been keeping up with the news over the last seven days? Test your knowledge of the latest top stories with our Quiz of the Week.

harvest.headline: Strange News: The weirdest stories of the week
harvest.summary: Shanequa has this week's Strange News, including very elaborate nail art, giant hailstones and a special delivery robot.

harvest.headline: Crew-12 Returns to Earth
harvest.summary: The SpaceX Crew Dragon Freedom spacecraft is seen as it lands with NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev aboard in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Los Angeles, Calif., Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026.

harvest.headline: Astronomers pinpoint the most distant fast radio burst ever detected
harvest.summary: Astronomers have detected and traced the most distant fast radio burst ever recorded, a powerful flash of radio waves that traveled for more than 10 billion years across the cosmos before reaching Earth.

harvest.headline: Artemis II Crew Moon Photo Annotations
harvest.summary: A visualization of a dark Moon eclipsing the Sun is marked with handwritten notes in this April 6, 2026, screenshot from an Artemis II crew member's tablet.

harvest.headline: Astronomers Solve Cosmic Cold Case with NASA Hubble Data
harvest.summary: This artist's concept depicts a possible explanation for the unusual chemical abundances NASA's Hubble Space Telescope detected in the HS 0209+0832 system: a second-generation planet orbiting the white dwarf star.
